items.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995…
items.q: So Gene was in the band, Gene Ammons. Gene Ammons was in the band, Lee Konitz was in the band, he was from Chicago, Eugene Wright was the bass player, and all the guys were just fantastic players.

ctx.x: Tell us about the first time you heard bebop. And do you remember what your reaction was?

Yeah I remember the first time I heard it. It wasn’t on — was it on records or not? I think it was probably the same time — I was in high school, or I had just graduated from high school I think, or maybe during my last year of high school. I really was getting into it. And so there was a saxophone player who was a good friend of mine who was really a Lester Young fanatic. And then he heard Charlie Parker, you know and he was talking about Charlie Parker. He says, “Oh you’ve got to listen to this.” So I went over…

Harold was a frustrated trumpet player himself. But he was a good musician, he knew about the theory of music. So he would trade bands a set of uniforms if they let him copy like some of the tunes from their book. Like we had tunes from Basie’s book, and remember the Billy Eckstine Big Band? We had some of those tunes. We had a couple of Dizzy’s tunes. We had a lot of Stan Kenton tunes, some Woody Herman things. The book was about that thick with all these things, you know all these charts. And we got all these…

items.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I was with this local big band, the one I was talking about that Gene Ammons played in. It was like the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band of today. All the heavyweights were in the band. Lee Konitz was in the band also.

ctx.x: Did you ever have occasion in those situations where someone would bring in a four page piece of music for the piano player, and you’re going “oh God, where’s the chord symbols?”

Oh, I feel the same way. I was never a fast sight reader. But you know as a kid I learned how to read music but it’s something that, you have to keep doing it. Once you stop, you’re going to not do it as well. And I stopped for years, because I went to the small band type way of playing. My reading was probably best right after high school and my first year of Roosevelt College. I was with this local big band, the one I was talking about that Gene Ammons played in. It was like the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band of…

blues, maybe that’s something in the back of my mind as to why I don’t have that much music. I have some tunes you know. Occasionally I let them work on a bebop tune and let an ensemble do it, but other than that I just sort of got away from it. I was never that interested in getting back to it. I was never interested; and doing studio work, which is probably the most lucrative part of the business you know. Like look at the studio musicians now, even those into retirement, man they have pensions in five and six…

items.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Both Jackie Cain and Junior Mance have told me about him

ctx.x: Both Jackie Cain and Junior Mance have told me about him, because they’re both a year younger than you are but basically came up at around the same time, so they both worked with that band, I guess, at some point or other.
Well, not when I was on it, I think Lou was the pianist, but I’m not sure of that now. I actually sang the blues [in] that band.
